plate_findings.evidence: central shadow of a detached vitreous body + in-text: retrolental space appeared densely filled with cells and opacities; hazy media with a Weiss ring in the mid-vitreous cavity

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Left infrared fundus from Fuchs Uveitis Syndrome article showing PVD shadow with in-text vitreous cells/opacities, supporting vocabulary vitreous opacities. B: B-scan in Fuchs Uveitis Syndrome case showing complete PVD with numerous fine echogenic vitreous opacities, direct vocabulary match with disease-focused title.
panels.attribution_text: Hedayatfar and Chee. Visual Blurring Following Posterior Vitreous Detachment in Fuchs Uveitis Syndrome.. Journal of ophthalmic & vision research 2026. doi:10.18502/jovr.v21.18382. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Left: The infrared image of the fundus reveals the central shadow of a detached vitreous body. Right: B-scan ultrasonography showing complete posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) with a shrunken vitreous body containing numerous fine echogenic opacities (gain: 110 dB).
in_text_mentions: without transillumination defect or PS. The crystalline lens was clear, but the retrolental space appeared densely filled with cells and opacities. Funduscopic examination showed hazy media with a Weiss ring in the mid-vitreous cavity. The retina was attached, with no chorioretinal scars. The optic disc was not swollen, with a cup-to-disc ratio of about 0.5. The infrared image of the fundus reveals the central shadow of a detached vitreous body. B-scan ultrasonography confirmed the presence of a complete PVD with a shrunken vitreous body containing numerous fine echogenic opacities [Figure 1].

plate_findings.evidence: shadow of the partially detached vitreous body over the macula

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (Left, Right). Left: Infrared fundus patient image in Fuchs Uveitis Syndrome article showing vitreous shadow/opacity over macula; in-text links echogenic opacity to accumulation of inflammatory cells, opacities and condensed vitreous strands on peripheral cortex. Right: B-scan ultrasonography patient image showing detached vitreous with echogenic opacities in thickened peripheral cortex, attributed in-text to inflammatory cells/opacities in Fuchs Uveitis Syndrome case.
panels.attribution_text: Hedayatfar and Chee. Visual Blurring Following Posterior Vitreous Detachment in Fuchs Uveitis Syndrome.. Journal of ophthalmic & vision research 2026. doi:10.18502/jovr.v21.18382. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Left: The infrared image of the fundus reveals the shadow of the partially detached vitreous body over the macula. Right: B-scan ultrasonography (gain: 79 dB) demonstrates a detached vitreous body that retains attachments to the peripheral retina (incomplete PVD). The echogenic opacities are mainly confined to the thickened, irregular peripheral vitreous cortex (arrows). Note the echo-free space between the detached vitreous body and the retina (asterisk).
in_text_mentions: mal, and OCT showed no macular edema. Direct funduscopy using a 90-diopter lens revealed a detached posterior hyaloid face. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated an incomplete PVD, with a thickened peripheral vitreous cortex contributing significantly to the echogenic opacity. This might imply the accumulation of inflammatory cells, opacities, and condensed vitreous strands on the peripheral vitreous cortex [Figure 2]. Three months later, she continued to experience unstable, blurred vision and disturbing floaters. Due to the lack of improvement, PPV was performed, restoring the vision to 20/20.
